newsitem.title: INDIA: Malaria called mounting world health problem.
newsitem.headline: Malaria called mounting world health problem.

text.p: Hundreds of scientists gathered on Monday in southern India to breathe new life into a global effort to control a resurgence of malaria, one of the world's greatest health threats.

Exactly 100 hundred years after the discovery that mosquitoes spread malaria, organisers of a five-day conference on parasitic illnesses said the disease has made a comeback and now contributes to three millions deaths a year.

"One hundred years ago there was hope this disease could soon be eliminated," World Health Organisation (WHO) South East Asian regional director Uton Rafei told the conference. "However, malaria is still with us as an enormous global health problem."
The second global conference on parasitic diseases, with about 700 delegates, was timed to coincide with the discovery in August 1897 by Sir Ronald Ross that mosquitoes transmit malaria.
Ross, who had suffered from malaria and was struck by cholera just before his discovery, made his breakthrough in the southern Indian city of Hyderabad, site of the conference.

One of the aims of the conference was to raise global awareness of the magnitude of the problem and the paucity of resources devoted to combating malaria compared with money spent on some diseases that are more prevalent in rich countries.
Malaria kills more people each year than have died from AIDS in the last 15, according to the New York-based Malaria Foundation.
About 40 percent of the world's population, or about 2.5 billion people, are at risk in more than 90 countries.
Most of the victims are children. Over one million children die of malaria each year -- four every minute -- and it is one of the five main causes of death among children under five.

Malaria, which was thought to be under control in much of the world only two decades ago, has become resistant to many drugs and insecticides. "We were complacent after our initial successes," V. Ramalingaswami of the All India Institute of Medical Sciences said.
Outbreaks have quadrupled in the last five years, with cases in the United States and Europe for the first time in decades.
High-risk groups are pregnant women, refugees, migrant workers and non-immune travellers. About 20 million Western tourists travel in regions prone to malaria every year.

Africa bears the brunt of the problem, with about 90 percent of all deaths by malaria. Malaria is present in South East Asia, India and South America and has spread to Azerbaijan, Sri Lanka and Turkey.

In India, malaria was almost wiped out but has staged a vicious comeback. Between 1950 and 1970, its eradication programme reduced annual infections from 75 million to 100,000, and deaths from 800,000 to virtually none.

But over the past two decades the trend has reversed, with four epidemics since 1994. In 1996, 2.85 million cases were reported, and the official death toll -- believed to be far below actual numbers -- was about 3,000. Now India accounts for 16 percent of the cases, second behind Africa.
"It is a major public health problem in India," the health minister of Andhra Pradesh state, Janardhan Reddy, said.
Organisers of the conference said there would be a call for greater cooperation between governments and drug companies to help discover new ways to combat malaria, including a vaccine.
